title: Part 1, Chapter 3
paragraphs: He woke up late the next day after a fitful sleep, but the sleep had done nothing for him. He woke up irritable, bad-tempered, and full of bile, and looked around his room with loathing. It was a tiny closet of a room, about six paces long. It looked wretched with its dusty yellow wallpaper peeling from the walls, and the ceiling was so low that anyone taller than average felt uncomfortable, constantly afraid of bumping their head. The furniture matched the room: three old chairs, wobbly at best; a painted table in the corner piled with a few notebooks and books, the thick dust on them proving they hadn't been touched in ages. A large, unwieldy sofa took up almost an entire wall and half the floor. It had once been upholstered in chintz but was now in tatters and served as Raskolnikov's bed. He often slept on it fully dressed, without sheets, wrapped in his old student's overcoat, his head on a single small pillow under which he piled all his linen -- clean and dirty -- as a makeshift bolster. A small table stood in front of the sofa.

It would have been hard to sink to a worse state of disorder, but in Raskolnikov's current frame of mind, the squalor actually suited him. He had completely withdrawn from everyone, like a turtle in its shell, and even the sight of the maid who occasionally came in to check on his room made him twitch with irritation. He was in the state that overtakes some monomaniacs who are entirely concentrated on one thing. His landlady had stopped sending him meals two weeks ago, and he hadn't bothered to argue about it, even though he went without dinner. Nastasya, the cook and only servant, was rather pleased with her lodger's mood and had given up cleaning his room altogether -- only once a week or so she would wander in with a broom. She was the one who woke him that day.
"Get up! Why are you still asleep?" she called to him. "It's past nine. I brought you some tea -- want a cup? You must be half-starved by now."
Raskolnikov opened his eyes, started, and recognized Nastasya.
"Is this from the landlady?" he asked, slowly sitting up on the sofa with a sickly expression.
"From the landlady -- sure!"
She set her own cracked teapot in front of him, full of weak, stale tea, and placed two yellowish lumps of sugar beside it.

"Here, Nastasya, take this," he said, fumbling in his pocket -- he had slept in his clothes -- and pulling out a handful of coppers. "Go buy me a loaf of bread. And get me a little sausage from the butcher's -- the cheapest one."
"I'll get you the bread right now. But wouldn't you rather have some cabbage soup instead of sausage? Good soup, from yesterday. I saved it for you, but you came home late. It's perfectly fine."
When the soup arrived and he began eating, Nastasya sat down beside him on the sofa and started chatting. She was a peasant woman from the country and very talkative.
"Praskovya Pavlovna, the landlady, is planning to report you to the police," she said.
He scowled.
"The police? What for?"
"You don't pay her and you won't move out. That's what she wants, obviously."
"Damn it, that's all I need," he muttered through clenched teeth. "No, that won't do... not right now. She's a fool," he added aloud. "I'll go talk to her today."

"She's a fool, no doubt about it, just like me. But if you're so clever, why are you just lying around with nothing to show for it? You used to go out and teach children, you said. So why aren't you doing anything now?"
"I am doing something..." Raskolnikov began sullenly and reluctantly.
"What are you doing?"
"Work..."
"What kind of work?"
"I'm thinking," he answered seriously, after a pause.
Nastasya doubled over with laughter. She was the type who laughed silently, her whole body quivering and shaking until she felt sick.
"And how much money have you made from your thinking?" she finally managed to say.
"You can't give lessons without boots. And I'm sick of it anyway."
"Don't turn your nose up at your bread and butter."
"They pay so little for lessons. What good are a few kopecks?" he replied reluctantly, as if answering his own thoughts.
"And you want a fortune handed to you all at once?"
He looked at her strangely.
"Yes, I want a fortune," he said firmly after a brief pause.
"Easy now -- you're scaring me! Should I get you the bread or not?"
"Whatever you like."
"Oh, I forgot! A letter came for you yesterday while you were out."
"A letter? For me? From whom?"
"I don't know. I paid the postman three kopecks of my own money for it. Will you pay me back?"
"Then bring it, for God's sake, bring it!" Raskolnikov cried, suddenly agitated. "Good God!"

A minute later the letter was in his hands. It was from his mother, from the province of R-----. He went pale as he took it. It had been a long time since he'd received any letter, but something else also stabbed at his heart.
"Nastasya, please leave me alone. Here are your three kopecks. Just go, please!"

The letter trembled in his hand. He didn't want to open it with her there -- he needed to be _alone_ with it. When Nastasya had gone, he raised the letter quickly to his lips and kissed it. Then he stared at the address, at the small, slanting handwriting, so dear and familiar, of the mother who had once taught him to read and write. He hesitated, almost afraid. Finally he opened it. It was thick and heavy, over two ounces -- two large sheets of notepaper covered with very small writing.

"My dear Rodya," his mother wrote. "It's been two months since I last wrote to you, and that has caused me pain and even kept me awake at night. But I'm sure you won't blame me for the silence -- it couldn't be helped. You know how much I love you. You are everything to Dounia and me -- our only hope, our only anchor. What grief it was for me to learn that you had left the university some months ago because you couldn't support yourself, and that you had lost your tutoring work and other income! How could I help you on my hundred-and-twenty-ruble pension? The fifteen rubles I sent you four months ago were borrowed, as you know, against my pension from Vassily Ivanovitch Vahrushin, a merchant here in town. He's a kindhearted man and was a friend of your father's. But having given him the right to collect my pension, I had to wait until the debt was repaid, which has only just happened. That's why I haven't been able to send you anything. But now, thank God, I believe I can send you more, and in fact we have reason to congratulate ourselves on a piece of good fortune, which I hasten to tell you about. First -- would you believe it, dear Rodya -- your sister has been living with me these last six weeks, and we won't be separated again. Thank God, her suffering is over. But let me tell you everything in order, so you know exactly what happened and everything we've been hiding from you. When you wrote two months ago that you'd heard Dounia was having a hard time at the Svidrigaïlovs', and asked me for details -- what could I have written? If I'd told you the whole truth, you would have dropped everything and come to us, even on foot -- I know your character and your feelings, and you would never stand for your sister being mistreated. I was desperate myself, but what could I do? Besides, I didn't know the full truth then. The biggest problem was that Dounia had received a hundred rubles in advance when she took the governess position, on condition that it would be deducted from her monthly salary. So she couldn't leave without repaying the debt. That sum -- now I can explain everything, my precious Rodya -- she had taken mainly to send you the sixty rubles you so desperately needed, which you received from us last year. We lied to you then, saying the money came from Dounia's savings, but it wasn't so. Now I'm telling you the truth because, thank God, things have changed for the better, and so you can see how much Dounia loves you and what kind of heart she has. At first, indeed, Mr. Svidrigaïlov treated her very rudely, making disrespectful and mocking remarks at the table.... But I don't want to go into all those painful details, since it's all over now. In short, despite the kind and generous behavior of Marfa Petrovna -- Mr. Svidrigaïlov's wife -- and the rest of the household, Dounia had a very hard time, especially when Mr. Svidrigaïlov, reverting to his old regimental habits, had been drinking. And how do you think it all turned out? Would you believe that the crazy fellow had been in love with Dounia from the very beginning but had hidden it behind rudeness and contempt? Perhaps he was ashamed of his own hopeless desires, horrified by himself, considering his age and the fact that he was a family man -- and that made him angry at Dounia. Or perhaps he hoped that his rude, sneering behavior would hide the truth from everyone else. But in the end he lost all self-control and had the audacity to make Dounia an open and shameless proposal, promising her all kinds of things, offering to abandon everything and take her to another estate or even abroad. You can imagine what she went through! She couldn't leave at once, not only because of the debt but also to spare Marfa Petrovna's feelings, since suspicions would have been aroused and Dounia would have been blamed for causing a family rift. It would have meant a terrible scandal for Dounia, too -- that was unavoidable. There were other reasons as well that made it impossible for Dounia to escape that awful house for another six weeks. You know Dounia -- you know how smart she is, how strong her will is. She can endure a great deal and even in the most desperate circumstances manages to stay resolute. She didn't even write to me about everything, for fear of upsetting me, though we wrote to each other constantly. It all ended very unexpectedly. Marfa Petrovna accidentally overheard her husband begging Dounia in the garden, and, putting entirely the wrong interpretation on the scene, blamed Dounia for everything. A terrible scene broke out between them right there in the garden. Marfa Petrovna went so far as to hit Dounia, refused to listen to a word, and screamed at her for a solid hour. Then she ordered Dounia packed off to me immediately in a peasant cart, into which they threw all her belongings -- clothes, linens, everything -- in a heap, without folding or packing any of it. And then a heavy rainstorm broke out, and Dounia, humiliated and shamed, had to ride with a peasant in an open cart for all seventeen versts into town. Now imagine what I could have written to you two months ago in response to your letter. I was in despair. I didn't dare write you the truth because you would have been miserable, outraged, and furious -- and what could you have done? You could only have ruined yourself, and Dounia wouldn't have allowed it. Yet how could I fill my letter with trivialities when my heart was so full of grief? For a whole month the town was buzzing with this scandal, and it reached the point where Dounia and I didn't dare go to church because of the contemptuous looks, the whispers, and even the remarks said aloud about us. All our acquaintances avoided us, no one would even greet us in the street, and I heard that some shopkeepers and clerks were planning to humiliate us by smearing our gates with tar, so that the landlord started telling us we'd have to move. All of this was Marfa Petrovna's doing -- she managed to slander Dounia and drag her name through the mud in every household. She knows everyone in the area, and that whole month she kept coming into town. Being rather talkative and fond of airing her family grievances -- which isn't right -- she spread her version of events not just through the town but across the entire district. It made me ill, but Dounia bore it better than I did. If you could have seen how she endured it all, comforting and cheering me! She's an angel! But by God's mercy, our suffering was cut short. Mr. Svidrigaïlov came to his senses, repented, and -- probably feeling sorry for Dounia -- presented Marfa Petrovna with complete and undeniable proof of Dounia's innocence in the form of a letter Dounia had been forced to write to him before Marfa Petrovna caught them in the garden. In this letter, which Mr. Svidrigaïlov had kept after Dounia left, she firmly refused all private meetings and personal explanations he had been begging for, and she reproached him with great passion for the vileness of his behavior toward Marfa Petrovna, reminding him that he was a father and head of a family, and telling him how despicable it was to torment a defenseless girl who was already unhappy enough. The letter, dear Rodya, was written so nobly and movingly that I wept as I read it and cannot read it to this day without tears. Furthermore, the testimony of the servants also cleared Dounia's name -- they had seen and known far more than Mr. Svidrigaïlov had supposed, as is always the case with servants. Marfa Petrovna was completely stunned, 'crushed again,' as she told us herself. But she was entirely convinced of Dounia's innocence. The very next day, a Sunday, she went straight to the cathedral, knelt down, and prayed with tears to Our Lady for the strength to bear this new trial and to do her duty. Then she came directly from the cathedral to us, told us the whole story, wept bitterly, and in full repentance embraced Dounia and begged her forgiveness. That same morning, without any delay, she went around to every house in town, and everywhere, shedding tears, she declared in the most flattering terms Dounia's innocence and the nobility of her feelings and conduct. She even showed and read aloud to everyone the letter Dounia had written to Mr. Svidrigaïlov, and allowed people to make copies of it -- which I must say strikes me as excessive. She spent several days this way, driving around the whole town, because some people had taken offense at not being visited first, so everyone had to take turns. In every house she was expected before she arrived, and everyone knew that on such and such a day Marfa Petrovna would be reading the letter in such and such a place, and people gathered for each reading, even those who had already heard it multiple times in their own homes and others'. In my opinion a great deal, a very great deal of this was unnecessary, but that is Marfa Petrovna's character. In any case, she succeeded in completely restoring Dounia's reputation, and all the shame of the affair fell squarely on her husband as the sole guilty party -- so much so that I actually began to feel sorry for him. It really was treating the crazy fellow too harshly. Dounia was immediately asked to give lessons in several families but refused. All at once, everyone started treating her with marked respect. All of this helped bring about the event that has, one might say, transformed our entire fortunes. You must know, dear Rodya, that Dounia has a suitor and has already agreed to marry him. I'm hurrying to tell you everything about it, and though it was arranged without your consent, I don't think you'll hold it against me or your sister -- you'll see that we couldn't wait to hear from you first. And you couldn't have judged the situation properly without being here. This is how it happened. He already holds the rank of counselor -- Pyotr Petrovitch Luzhin -- and is a distant relative of Marfa Petrovna, who played an active role in arranging the match. It began with him expressing through her a desire to meet us. He was properly received, had coffee with us, and the very next day sent us a letter in which he very courteously proposed and asked for a prompt answer. He is a very busy man and in a great hurry to get to Petersburg, so every moment matters to him. Of course we were surprised at first -- it had all happened so fast and unexpectedly. We spent the whole day thinking and talking it over. He's a man of means, reliable, with two government positions and an established fortune. It's true he's forty-five, but he's fairly presentable in appearance and might still be considered attractive to women -- altogether a very respectable and proper man, though perhaps a bit gloomy and somewhat conceited. But that may just be the first impression. And please, dear Rodya, when he arrives in Petersburg shortly, don't judge him too hastily or harshly, as you tend to do, if something about him doesn't appeal to you right away. I say this even though I'm sure he'll make a good impression on you. Besides, to truly understand any person, you must be patient and careful, and avoid forming hasty opinions that are hard to correct later. Pyotr Petrovitch, judging by many indications, is a thoroughly estimable man. At his first visit he told us he was a practical man but still shared, as he put it, many of the convictions of 'our most progressive generation' and opposed all prejudices. He said a good deal more -- he seems a bit conceited and likes an audience -- but this is hardly a serious fault. I understood very little of it, of course, but Dounia explained to me that though he isn't a highly educated man, he's intelligent and seems good-natured. You know your sister's character, Rodya. She's resolute, sensible, patient, and generous -- but she also has a passionate heart, as I know well. Of course there's no great love on either side, but Dounia is a smart girl with the heart of an angel, and she will make it her duty to make her husband happy, while he in turn will make her happiness his concern. We have no good reason to doubt that, though it must be admitted the whole thing was arranged rather quickly. He's also a very prudent man, and he'll surely see that his own happiness depends on making Dounia happy. As for certain shortcomings of character, certain habits, and even some differences of opinion -- inevitable in even the happiest marriages -- Dounia says she's confident in herself and sees nothing to worry about, that she can put up with a great deal so long as the relationship is honorable and straightforward. He did strike me at first as somewhat brusque, but that may well come from his being an outspoken man -- and no doubt that's how it is. For instance, on his second visit, after receiving Dounia's acceptance, he mentioned in conversation that even before meeting Dounia, he had decided to marry a respectable girl without a dowry, and, above all, one who had experienced poverty, because, as he explained, a man ought not to be indebted to his wife, and it is better for a wife to look upon her husband as her benefactor. I should add that he expressed it more politely than I've put it here -- I've forgotten his exact words and only remember the gist. And besides, it clearly wasn't said deliberately but slipped out in the heat of conversation, and he tried to walk it back afterward. Still, it struck me as somewhat rude, and I told Dounia so. But Dounia was annoyed and replied that 'words are not deeds,' which is of course perfectly true. Dounia didn't sleep at all the night before she decided. Thinking I was asleep, she got out of bed and paced the room all night. Finally she knelt before the icon and prayed long and fervently. In the morning she told me she had made up her mind.

"I mentioned already that Pyotr Petrovitch is about to leave for Petersburg, where he has a great deal of business and wants to open a law office. He has spent many years handling civil and commercial cases, and just recently won an important one. He needs to be in Petersburg because he has a major case before the Senate. So, dear Rodya, he could be enormously useful to you, in every way, and Dounia and I have agreed that starting right now you could consider your career launched and your future settled. Oh, if only this comes true! It would be such a blessing that we could only see it as Providence. Dounia dreams of nothing else. We've even ventured to mention the subject to Pyotr Petrovitch. He answered cautiously, saying that since he needs a secretary, it would be better to pay a salary to a relative than a stranger -- provided the person was qualified (as if there could be any doubt about you!) -- but he wondered whether your university studies would leave you time for office work. The matter was dropped for the moment, but Dounia can think of nothing else. She's been in a kind of fever these past few days and has already drawn up a whole plan for you to eventually become an associate and even a partner in Pyotr Petrovitch's practice, which seems perfectly feasible since you're a law student. I completely agree with her, Rodya, and share all her plans and hopes. I think there's every chance of them coming true. Despite Pyotr Petrovitch's understandable caution -- he doesn't know you yet -- Dounia is firmly convinced she can achieve everything through her good influence on her future husband. That's what she's counting on. Of course we're careful not to mention these longer-range plans to Pyotr Petrovitch, especially the idea of making you his partner. He's a practical man and might dismiss it as pure fantasy. Neither Dounia nor I have said a word about our hope that he'll help with your university expenses -- partly because it will happen naturally in time, and he'll no doubt offer it himself without being asked (how could he refuse Dounia?), especially since you could become his right hand at the office and receive the help not as charity but as an earned salary. Dounia wants to arrange it just this way, and I fully agree. We also haven't raised it for another reason: I particularly wanted you to meet him on equal footing. When Dounia spoke enthusiastically about you, he said you can never judge a person without meeting them in person, and that he looks forward to forming his own opinion when he meets you. You know, my dear Rodya, I think perhaps for certain reasons -- nothing to do with Pyotr Petrovitch, just my own personal, perhaps old-womanish ideas -- it might be better for me to go on living by myself rather than with them after the wedding. I'm sure he'll be generous and considerate enough to invite me to stay with my daughter, and if he hasn't mentioned it yet, it's simply been taken for granted. But I'll refuse. I've noticed more than once in life that husbands and mothers-in-law don't always get along smoothly, and I don't want to be even the slightest burden to anyone. For my own sake, too, I'd rather remain independent, as long as I have a crust of bread and children like you and Dounia. If possible, I'd settle somewhere near you. And now for the best news, dear Rodya, which I've saved for last: we may all be together very soon and may embrace each other after a separation of nearly three years! It is _definite_ that Dounia and I are coming to Petersburg -- exactly when I'm not sure, but very soon, possibly within a week. It all depends on Pyotr Petrovitch, who will let us know once he's had a chance to get settled in Petersburg. To suit his arrangements, he wants the ceremony to take place as soon as possible, even before the Fast of Our Lady in August if it can be managed, or if that's too soon, then immediately after. Oh, how happy I'll be to hold you in my arms! Dounia is wild with excitement at the thought of seeing you -- she said in jest the other day that she'd marry Pyotr Petrovitch for that alone. She's an angel! She's not writing to you now -- she told me to say that she has so much, so much to tell you that she won't even try to put pen to paper yet, since a few lines would say nothing and would only upset her. She sends you her love and countless kisses. And even though we'll be seeing each other so soon, I'll try to send you some money in the next day or two. Now that everyone knows Dounia is marrying Pyotr Petrovitch, my credit has improved, and I'm sure Afanasy Ivanovitch will lend me up to seventy-five rubles against my pension, so I may be able to send you twenty-five or even thirty. I'd send more, but I'm worried about our travel costs. Though Pyotr Petrovitch has kindly taken on part of the expense -- he's arranged for our bags and large trunk to be shipped through some acquaintances -- we'll still need money when we arrive in Petersburg, where we can't turn up without a kopeck, at least for the first few days. Dounia and I have calculated everything down to the last penny, and the trip won't cost very much. It's only ninety versts to the railway, and we've arranged with a driver we know to be ready. From there, Dounia and I can travel quite comfortably in third class. So I may well be able to send you not twenty-five but thirty rubles. But enough -- I've already filled two sheets and there's no room left. Our whole story -- but so many events have happened! And now, my precious Rodya, I embrace you and send you a mother's blessing until we meet. Love Dounia, your sister, Rodya -- love her as she loves you, and know that she loves you beyond everything, more than herself. She is an angel, and you, Rodya, are everything to us -- our only hope, our only comfort. If only you are happy, we will be happy. Do you still pray, Rodya? Do you still believe in the mercy of our Creator and Redeemer? I'm afraid in my heart that the new spirit of unbelief so widespread today may have touched you. If so, I pray for you. Remember, dear boy, how in your childhood, when your father was alive, you used to lisp your prayers at my knee, and how happy we all were then. Goodbye until we meet. I embrace you warmly, warmly, with so many kisses.
"Yours until death,
"PULCHERIA RASKOLNIKOV."

Almost from the very first line, Raskolnikov's face was wet with tears. But when he finished reading, his face was pale and contorted, and a bitter, angry, malicious smile played on his lips. He laid his head on his threadbare, dirty pillow and brooded, brooded for a long time. His heart was pounding and his mind was in turmoil. Finally the cramped little yellow room -- like a cupboard or a box -- became unbearable. His eyes and his mind craved open space. He grabbed his hat and went out, this time without the fear of running into anyone -- he had forgotten that fear entirely. He headed toward Vassilyevsky Island, walking along Vassilyevsky Prospect as though he had some urgent business. But as usual, he didn't notice where he was going, muttering and even talking aloud to himself, startling passersby. Many of them assumed he was drunk.
